          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The instant writ petition under Article 32 of
the  Constitution  of  India  has  been  filed  by  the
petitioners seeking directions to the respondents to
implement provisions of the National Commission for
Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021(hereinafter
being referred to as the ‘Act, 2021’) in its true
letter and spirit for the regulation and maintenance of
standards for education and services by allied and
healthcare professionals in India.
4

--- Page 28 ---
This  Court  on  12th August,  2024  passed  the
following order:-
1. The  application  for  impleadment  of  the
Chairperson  of  the  National  Commission  for
Allied  and  Healthcare  Professions  as  a
respondent is allowed. 
2. The  National  Commission  for  Allied  and
Healthcare Professions Act 2021 was enacted by
Parliament on 24 March 2021. Upon notification
on 28 March 2021 in the Gazette of India, it
came into force on 25 May 2021. 
3. The grievance in these proceedings is that
inspite of the passage of over three years from
the  enforcement  of  the  Act,  most  of  its
provisions have not been implemented. Moreover,
it  has  been  submitted  that  the  maximum
permissible extensions were availed of by the
Centre and the States under Section 69. Though
the Union Government has set up a National
Commission, it appears that there is no further
progress. 
4. Notice was issued by this Court on 22 September
2023. Out of twenty-eight States and eight
Union Territories, only fourteen States have
constituted State Councils. These States are: 
(i)      Himachal Pradesh; 
(ii) Odisha; 
(iii) West Bengal; 
(iv) Assam; 
(v) Uttarakhand; 
(vi) Uttar Pradesh; 
(vii) Kerala; 
(viii) Andhra Pradesh; 
(ix) Mizoram; 
(x) Nagaland; 
(xi) Sikkim; 
(xii) Telangana; 
(xiii) Tripura; and 
(xiv) Arunachal Pradesh. 
Even the State Councils which have been set up,
it has been urged, are not functional. 
5. The directions which have been sought at the
present stage are: 
(i) Constitution of State Councils by all
States  and  Union  Territories  after
framing rules under Section 68(2)(a-e);
(ii) Framing of regulations by the Central
Government  under  Section  66  for
5

--- Page 29 ---
discharge of functions as provided in
Section 11;
(iii) Constitution of Professional Councils
as required by Section 10;
(iv) Constitution of Advisory Councils as
required by Section 12; and
(v) Constitution of Autonomous Boards by
State Governments under Section 29. 
6. Though this Court entertained the petition in
September  2023,  the  fact  remains  that  the
provisions of the Act have still not been
implemented.  The  proliferation  of  illegal
allied healthcare educational institutions and
affiliating  bodies  is  a  mater  of  serious
concern.  The  Parliamentary  legislation  was
enacted to provide a legislative framework to
protect  the  public  interest  against  the
proliferation  of  illegal  institutions  and
bodies. 
7. Despite the passage of three years since the
enactment of the law, both the Union Government
and the State Governments have yet to discharge
their statutory responsibilities. No counter
affidavit  has  been  filed  by  the  Union
Government.
8. Mr  Vikramjit  Banerjee,  Additional  Solicitor
General states that a counter would be filed
within  a  period  of  two  weeks.  We  see  no
justification for the Union Government not to
have taken action to respond to the proceedings
after service of notice. Similarly, there is no
justification available on the record for not
implementing  the  provisions  of  the
Parliamentary legislation. 
9. We accordingly direct as follows: 
(i) The  Union  Government  and  the  State
Governments shall on or before 12 October
2024, take necessary steps to implement the
provisions of the Act;
(ii) The  Secretary  in  the  Union  Ministry  of
Health and Family Welfare shall within a
period of two weeks from the date of this
order, convene an online meeting of all the
Secretaries  in  the  State  Ministries  of
Health and Family Welfare and a definite
road  map  for  compliance  with  the  above
directions  shall  be  laid  down  for  the
purpose  of  ensuring  that  the  requisite
steps to implement the provisions of the
Act are taken, infrastructure is set up by
all  the  States  and  the  institutions
contemplated by the Act are made functional
6

--- Page 30 ---
not only in letter but in spirit as well by
taking necessary action in that regard;
(iii) All the States/Union Territories shall file
compliance reports to the Secretary in the
Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
by the next date of hearing; and
(iv) The compliance reports shall be compiled in
a  tabulated  statement  and  be  presented
before this Court on behalf of the Union
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by
the next date of listing.
10. Failing  compliance,  all  the  States/Union
Territories and the Union Government are put
on notice that this Court may have to take
recourse to steps for failure to abide by the
directions and to implement the Parliamentary
legislation.
11. List the Petition on 18 October 2024.
Today,  during  the  course  of  proceedings,
learned counsel for the petitioners urged that the
regulations under the Act, 2021 have not been framed
by the National Commission.  Only 15 States have
framed the Rules and formed the councils but till date
the  same  are  either  not  being  notified  or  are
virtually non-functional.  
It is further submitted that the absence of
regulations and non-notification of the councils is
leading to continued violation of the Act, 2021.  It
is thus submitted that the respondents are not only
violating the provisions of the Act, 2021 but are also
acting  in  contravention  of  the  order  dated  12 th
August, 2024.
Shri Vikramjit  Banerjee, learned  ASG urged
that  the  obligation  to  carry  out  the  necessary
7

--- Page 31 ---
formalities under the Act, 2021 are mostly on the
States and hence, they should be directed to ensure
compliance of the Act, 2021 and this Court’s order.
Taking note of the fact that till date the
directions given in the order dated 12 th August, 2024
have not been fully complied either by the National
Commission or by the States, we direct the Chief
Secretaries and the Health Secretaries of all the
States and the Union Territories and so also the
National Commission to file affidavits of compliance
giving details of the notification of the councils,
framing of the rules under Section 68(2)(a-e) and
framing of the regulations under Section 66 by the
National Commission and with regard to all other
actions required to be taken under order dated 12 th
August, 2024.
A  copy  of  this  order  shall  be  forthwith
transmitted  to  Chief  Secretaries  and  Health
Secretaries of all the States, the administrators of
the Union Territories and the National Commission for
ensuring  compliance  and  filing  the  compliance
affidavits by the next date failing which this Court
shall be compelled to require personal attendance of
all the officers concerned.
List this matter on 22nd September, 2026.
(SHIPRA NARANG)                           (RANJANA SHAILEY)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT                     ASSISTANT REGISTRAR
8

--- Page 32 ---

4) The facts giving rise to the present appeal are as follows:

2 In short “detenu”

4.1) On 16.05.2024, Crime No. 640 of 2024 came to be

order dated 08.04.2026 impugned before us, the High

4.12) The High Court principally examined the effect of the

5) The appellant has now approached this Court, assailing the

the order of detention and the order of confirmation.  
 
6) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the 
appellant and the learned counsel appearing for the 
respondent State, and we have perused the material placed 
on record. 
 
ANALYSIS 
7) Before we turn to the questions that arise in this appeal, it is 
necessary to bear in mind the nature of the jurisdiction that 
is invoked when an order of preventive detention is called in 
question. Such an order is not passed upon proof of guilt 
established at a trial, but upon the subjective satisfaction of 
the Detaining Authority that the detention of a person is 
necessary to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial 

--- Page 59 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 5 
 
to the object which the PITNDPS Act seeks to serve. It is not 
for this Court, while examining the legality of such an order, 
to sit in judgment over the sufficiency of the material on which 
the satisfaction is founded, or to substitute its own opinion 
for that of the Detaining Authority on the question whether 
the detenu ought to have been detained. To that extent the 
area of judicial review is a narrow one. 
 
8) That narrowness, however, does not reduce judicial scrutiny 
to an empty formality. Preventive detention permits the 
deprivation of the liberty of a person on the basis of what he 
may do and not on the basis of what he has been found to 
have done. A power o f that description, which is a serious 
inroad into the personal liberty guaranteed by Article 21 of 
the Constitution of India (hereinafter referred to as the 
"Constitution"), can be sustained only if it is exercised in strict 
conformity with the conditions which the Constitution and the 
statute have prescribed for its exercise. Those conditions are 
not technicalities to be observed in form and disregarded in 
substance. They constitute the only safeguards available to a 
person who is detained without the benefit of a trial, and they 
are, therefore, to be enforced with corresponding strictness. 
 
9) In the present appeal, the question which arises before us is 
whether the constitutional safeguards attaching to the right 
of the detenu to make a representation against his preventive 
detention were duly observed. We propose to consider this 

--- Page 60 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 6 
 
question after setting out the constitutional and statutory 
framework within which it falls to be answered. 
THE CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY FRAMEWORK 
10) The Constitution, while permitting preventive detention, does 
not leave the person detained wholly without protection. 
Clause (5) of Article 22 of the Constitution provides as follows: 
 
"22. (5) When any person is detained in pursuance of 
an order made under any law providing for 
preventive detention, the authority making the order 
shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such 
person the grounds on which the order has been 
made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of 
making a representation against the order." 
 
 
11) Two distinct obligations flow from this provision, and both are 
cast upon the authority making the order. The first is to 
communicate to the detenu, as soon as may be, the grounds 
on which the order of detention has been made. The second 
is to afford him t he earliest opportunity of making a 
representation against the order. The right to make a 
representation would be an empty right if it did not carry with 
it a corresponding obligation on the part of the authority to 
consider that representation, and to consider it independently 
and with reasonable despatch. The communication of the 
grounds and the opportunity to represent are not ends in 
themselves. They exist so that the detenu may effectively 
resist his detention at the earliest point of time, and any 

--- Page 61 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 7 
 
failure which renders that opportunity illusory strikes at the 
root of the detention.  
 
12) The PITNDPS Act is a law providing for preventive detention 
within the meaning of Article 22  of the Constitution . The 
power to detain is conferred by Section 3, sub -section (1) of 
PITNDPS Act which is in the following terms insofar as it is 
material: 
 
"3. (1) The Central Government or a State 
Government, or any officer of the Central 
Government, not below the rank of a Joint Secretary 
to that Government, specially empowered for the 
purposes of this section by that Government, or any 
officer of a State Government, not below the rank of a 
Secretary to that Government, specially empowered 
for the purposes of this section by that Government, 
may, if satisfied, with respect to any person that, 
with a view to preventing him from engaging in illicit 
traffic in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, 
it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that 
such person be detained." 
 
13) It is necessary to understand that the power under Section 
3(1) of PITNDPS Act may be exercised either by the State 
Government itself or by an officer of the State Government 
who is not below the rank of a Secretary and who has been 
specially empowered in that behalf. When the power is 
exercised by such an officer, the satisfaction which the section 
requires is the satisfaction of that officer, arrived at upon his 
own application of mind, and the order is his order and not 
that of the Government. This distinction is not one of mere 

--- Page 62 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 8 
 
form, and its significance will become apparent when we come 
to consider the manner in which the representation of the 
detenu was dealt with in the present case. 
 
14) The further stages of a detention under the PITNDPS Act are 
regulated by Section 9, which gives effect to the requirement 
of Article 22 of the Constitution that no detention shall 
ordinarily continue beyond three months unless an Advisory 
Board has reported that there is sufficient cause for it. Under 
clause (b) of Section 9, the appropriate Government is 
required to make a reference to the Advisory Board within five 
weeks from the date of detention. Under clause (c), the 
Advisory Board is required to consider the reference and to 
submit its report within eleven weeks from the date of 
detention, specifying its opinion as to whether or not there is 
sufficient cause for the detention. Under clause (f), where the 
Advisory Board has reported that there is sufficient cause, the 
appropriate Government may confirm the order of detention, 
and where it has reported that there is no sufficient cause, 
the appropriate Government is bound to revoke the order and 
to release the person forthwith. 
 
15) One feature of this statutory scheme is of particular 
significance in the present case. The consideration of the 
detenu's representation by an authority competent to revoke 
the detention stands on a footing distinct from the 
consideration of the case by the Advisory Board. The opinion 
of the Advisory Board is directed to the question whether there 

--- Page 63 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 9 
 
is sufficient cause for the detention, whereas consideration of 
the representation gives effect to the constitutional right 
guaranteed by Article 22(5) of the Constitution. One cannot 
substitute the other, and compliance with the obligation to 
refer the ma tter to the Advisory Board does not absolve the 
competent authority of its independent obligation to consider 
the representation with the expedition which the 
constitutional guarantee requires. 
 
THE RIGHT OF REPRESENTATION AND ITS CONSIDERATION 
 
16) The issue which requires determination concerns the right of 
the detenu to make a representation against the order of 
detention and the manner in which the representation 
actually made by him was dealt with. This ground goes to the 
legality of the detention as a whole, and for the reasons that 
follow we are of the opinion that it is well founded. 
 
17) It has already been noted that Article 22(5) of the Constitution 
casts upon the authority making the order of detention two 
distinct obligations, and that the second of them is to afford 
the detenu the earliest opportunity of making a representation 
against the order. That opportunity carries with it, as a 
necessary con comitant, the obligation of the authority to 
inform the detenu of the persons or bodies to whom he may 
address his representation. Where the order of detention has 
been made by an officer specially empowered under Section 
3(1) of the PITNDPS Act , the detenu is entitled to make a 

--- Page 64 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 10 
 
representation to that officer, who made the order and who is 
competent to revoke it, and he must be informed of that right. 
That such a right, distinct from the right to represent to the 
State Government, to the Advisory Board and to the Central 
Government, enures to the detenu and must be made known 
to him, was settled by a Constitution Bench of this Court in 
Kamleshkumar Ishwardas Patel v. Union of India 4,  in 
relation to this very Act among others. The failure to inform 
the detenu of it renders the opportunity to represent 
incomplete and deprives him of a valuable safeguard. 
 
18) In the present case, the order of detention was made by the 
Detaining Authority in exercise of the power conferred upon 
an officer specially empowered under Section 3(1) of the 
PITNDPS Act. The detenu was informed that he could make 
representations to the State Government, the Advisory Board 
and the Central Government. He was not separately informed 
that he was entitled to make a representation to the officer 
who had made the order of detention in exercise of the 
specially conferred statutory power. The omi ssion is evident 
from the detention order itself. The fact that the detenu 
nevertheless addressed one of his representations to the 
Detaining Authority cannot cure the failure to inform him of 
that constitutional right. The obligation was upon the 
authority to communicate the right and could not depend 
upon whether the detenu independently became aware of it. 
 
 
4 (1995) 4 SCC 51 

--- Page 65 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 11 
 
19) The matter does not rest with the failure to inform the detenu 
of his right. The representation addressed to the Detaining 
Authority was submitted on 13.02.2026. The case was 
thereafter referred to the Advisory Board on 16.02.2026. The 
Advisory Board submi tted its report only on 13.03.2026. 
Neither the order of confirmation nor the counter affidavit filed 
before this Court discloses any separate consideration or 
decision upon the representation by the Detaining Authority 
in exercise of its statutory power. On the contrary, the case of 
the respondents is that the representation was examined 
together with the opinion of the Advisory Board and the other 
connected documents. This sequence indicates that the 
representation was kept pending until the Advisory Board had 
rendered its opinion and was thereafter dealt with as part of 
the governmental exercise of confirmation. The consideration 
of a representation under Article 22(5) and the examination 
undertaken by the Advisory Board are distinct constitutional 
processes. The opinion of the Advisory Board cannot 
substitute the independent consideration required from an 
authority competent to revoke the detention. This principle 
stands recognised by this Court in Gracy v. State of Kerala5, 
and K.M. Abdulla Kunhi v. Union of India 6. The record in 
the present case does not disclose the distinct and 
independent decision which the constitutional guarantee 
required. 
 
 
5 (1991) 2 SCC 1 
6 (1991) 1 SCC 476 

--- Page 66 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 12 
 
20) There is also an unexplained delay in dealing with the 
representation. Even if the order of confirmation dated 
19.03.2026 is treated as the first decision upon the 
representation dated 13.02.2026, a period of 34 days had 
elapsed before such consideration. A further period of eight 
days elapsed before the rejection was communicated to the 
detenu on 27.03.2026. No separate order deciding the 
representation has been placed before us. Nor has any 
satisfactory or day-to-day explanation been furnished for the 
time taken either to consider the representation or to 
communicate the decision. The general statement that the 
representation was examined together with the opinion of the 
Advisory Board does n ot explain the delay. It instead 
reinforces the conclusion that the representation was not 
treated as an independent constitutional process requiring 
immediate attention. 
 
21) We accordingly hold that the safeguards attaching to the right 
of the detenu to make a representation against his detention 
were not observed. The detenu was not informed of his right 
to represent to the Detaining Authority who had made the 
order. The record does not disclose any independent decision 
upon the representation by the Detaining Authority in 
exercise of his own statutory power. The consideration 
disclosed by the respondents was undertaken only as part of 
the subsequent confirmation exercise, and  even that 
consideration was attended by an unexplained delay. These 
infirmities violate Article 22(5) of the Constitution and are 

--- Page 67 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 13 
 
sufficient to render the continued detention of the detenu 
illegal. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
22) The infirmities noted above are not mere technical or 
procedural irregularities capable of being cured by 
substantial compliance. They concern the enforcement of the 
constitutional right guaranteed by Article 22(5) to a person 
detained without trial. Once a mandatory constitut ional 
safeguard governing preventive detention is found to have 
been violated, the continued detention cannot be sustained . 
The High Court did not examine whether the representation 
submitted by the detenu received the independent and 
expeditious consideration required by Article 22(5) of the 
Constitution. Since that issue bears directly upon the legality 
of the continued deten tion, the judgment of the High Court 
cannot be sustained. 
 
23) Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order 
dated 08.04.2026 passed by the High Court in Writ Petition 
(Criminal) No. 566 of 2026 is set aside. The order of detention 
dated 13.01.2026 passed against the detenu under Section 
3(1) of the PITND PS Act and the order of confirmation dated 
19.03.2026 are quashed. 
 
24) The detenu, Muhammed Rafi, shall be set at liberty forthwith, 
unless his detention or custody is required in connection with 
any other case. 

--- Page 68 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 14 
 
 
25) Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. There 
shall be no order as to costs.

ANALYSIS

necessary to bear in mind the nature of the jurisdiction that

--- Page 73 ---

to the object which the PITNDPS Act seeks to serve. It is not

for that of the Detaining Authority on the question whether 
the detenu ought to have been detained. To that extent the

are, therefore, to be enforced with corresponding strictness.

whether the constitutional safeguards attaching to the right 
of the detenu to make a representation against his preventive 
detention were duly observed. We propose to consider this

question after setting out the constitutional and statutory 
framework within which it falls to be answered. 
THE CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY FRAMEWORK 
10) The Constitution, while permitting preventive detention, does 
not leave the person detained wholly without protection. 
Clause (5) of Article 22 of the Constitution provides as follows: 
 
"22. (5) When any person is detained in pursuance of 
an order made under any law providing for 
preventive detention, the authority making the order 
shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such 
person the grounds on which the order has been 
made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of 
making a representation against the order." 
 
 
11) Two distinct obligations flow from this provision, and both are 
cast upon the authority making the order. The first is to 
communicate to the detenu, as soon as may be, the grounds 
on which the order of detention has been made. The second 
is to afford him t he earliest opportunity of making a 
representation against the order. The right to make a 
representation would be an empty right if it did not carry with 
it a corresponding obligation on the part of the authority to 
consider that representation, and to consider it independently 
and with reasonable despatch. The communication of the 
grounds and the opportunity to represent are not ends in 
themselves. They exist so that the detenu may effectively 
resist his detention at the earliest point of time, and any 

--- Page 75 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 7 
 
failure which renders that opportunity illusory strikes at the 
root of the detention.  
 
12) The PITNDPS Act is a law providing for preventive detention 
within the meaning of Article 22  of the Constitution . The 
power to detain is conferred by Section 3, sub -section (1) of 
PITNDPS Act which is in the following terms insofar as it is 
material: 
 
"3. (1) The Central Government or a State 
Government, or any officer of the Central 
Government, not below the rank of a Joint Secretary 
to that Government, specially empowered for the 
purposes of this section by that Government, or any 
officer of a State Government, not below the rank of a 
Secretary to that Government, specially empowered 
for the purposes of this section by that Government, 
may, if satisfied, with respect to any person that, 
with a view to preventing him from engaging in illicit 
traffic in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, 
it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that 
such person be detained." 
 
13) It is necessary to understand that the power under Section 
3(1) of PITNDPS Act may be exercised either by the State 
Government itself or by an officer of the State Government 
who is not below the rank of a Secretary and who has been 
specially empowered in that behalf. When the power is 
exercised by such an officer, the satisfaction which the section 
requires is the satisfaction of that officer, arrived at upon his 
own application of mind, and the order is his order and not 
that of the Government. This distinction is not one of mere 

--- Page 76 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 8 
 
form, and its significance will become apparent when we come 
to consider the manner in which the representation of the 
detenu was dealt with in the present case. 
 
14) The further stages of a detention under the PITNDPS Act are 
regulated by Section 9, which gives effect to the requirement 
of Article 22 of the Constitution that no detention shall 
ordinarily continue beyond three months unless an Advisory 
Board has reported that there is sufficient cause for it. Under 
clause (b) of Section 9, the appropriate Government is 
required to make a reference to the Advisory Board within five 
weeks from the date of detention. Under clause (c), the 
Advisory Board is required to consider the reference and to 
submit its report within eleven weeks from the date of 
detention, specifying its opinion as to whether or not there is 
sufficient cause for the detention. Under clause (f), where the 
Advisory Board has reported that there is sufficient cause, the 
appropriate Government may confirm the order of detention, 
and where it has reported that there is no sufficient cause, 
the appropriate Government is bound to revoke the order and 
to release the person forthwith. 
 
15) One feature of this statutory scheme is of particular 
significance in the present case. The consideration of the 
detenu's representation by an authority competent to revoke 
the detention stands on a footing distinct from the 
consideration of the case by the Advisory Board. The opinion 
of the Advisory Board is directed to the question whether there 

--- Page 77 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 9 
 
is sufficient cause for the detention, whereas consideration of 
the representation gives effect to the constitutional right 
guaranteed by Article 22(5) of the Constitution. One cannot 
substitute the other, and compliance with the obligation to 
refer the ma tter to the Advisory Board does not absolve the 
competent authority of its independent obligation to consider 
the representation with the expedition which the 
constitutional guarantee requires. 
 
THE RIGHT OF REPRESENTATION AND ITS CONSIDERATION 
 
16) The issue which requires determination concerns the right of 
the detenu to make a representation against the order of 
detention and the manner in which the representation 
actually made by him was dealt with. This ground goes to the 
legality of the detention as a whole, and for the reasons that 
follow we are of the opinion that it is well founded. 
 
17) It has already been noted that Article 22(5) of the Constitution 
casts upon the authority making the order of detention two 
distinct obligations, and that the second of them is to afford 
the detenu the earliest opportunity of making a representation 
against the order. That opportunity carries with it, as a 
necessary con comitant, the obligation of the authority to 
inform the detenu of the persons or bodies to whom he may 
address his representation. Where the order of detention has 
been made by an officer specially empowered under Section 
3(1) of the PITNDPS Act , the detenu is entitled to make a 

--- Page 78 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 10 
 
representation to that officer, who made the order and who is 
competent to revoke it, and he must be informed of that right. 
That such a right, distinct from the right to represent to the 
State Government, to the Advisory Board and to the Central 
Government, enures to the detenu and must be made known 
to him, was settled by a Constitution Bench of this Court in 
Kamleshkumar Ishwardas Patel v. Union of India 4,  in 
relation to this very Act among others. The failure to inform 
the detenu of it renders the opportunity to represent 
incomplete and deprives him of a valuable safeguard. 
 
18) In the present case, the order of detention was made by the 
Detaining Authority in exercise of the power conferred upon 
an officer specially empowered under Section 3(1) of the 
PITNDPS Act. The detenu was informed that he could make 
representations to the State Government, the Advisory Board 
and the Central Government. He was not separately informed 
that he was entitled to make a representation to the officer 
who had made the order of detention in exercise of the 
specially conferred statutory power. The omi ssion is evident 
from the detention order itself. The fact that the detenu 
nevertheless addressed one of his representations to the 
Detaining Authority cannot cure the failure to inform him of 
that constitutional right. The obligation was upon the 
authority to communicate the right and could not depend 
upon whether the detenu independently became aware of it. 
 
 
4 (1995) 4 SCC 51 

--- Page 79 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 11 
 
19) The matter does not rest with the failure to inform the detenu 
of his right. The representation addressed to the Detaining 
Authority was submitted on 13.02.2026. The case was 
thereafter referred to the Advisory Board on 16.02.2026. The 
Advisory Board submi tted its report only on 13.03.2026. 
Neither the order of confirmation nor the counter affidavit filed 
before this Court discloses any separate consideration or 
decision upon the representation by the Detaining Authority 
in exercise of its statutory power. On the contrary, the case of 
the respondents is that the representation was examined 
together with the opinion of the Advisory Board and the other 
connected documents. This sequence indicates that the 
representation was kept pending until the Advisory Board had 
rendered its opinion and was thereafter dealt with as part of 
the governmental exercise of confirmation. The consideration 
of a representation under Article 22(5) and the examination 
undertaken by the Advisory Board are distinct constitutional 
processes. The opinion of the Advisory Board cannot 
substitute the independent consideration required from an 
authority competent to revoke the detention. This principle 
stands recognised by this Court in Gracy v. State of Kerala5, 
and K.M. Abdulla Kunhi v. Union of India 6. The record in 
the present case does not disclose the distinct and 
independent decision which the constitutional guarantee 
required. 
 
 
5 (1991) 2 SCC 1 
6 (1991) 1 SCC 476 

--- Page 80 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 12 
 
20) There is also an unexplained delay in dealing with the 
representation. Even if the order of confirmation dated 
19.03.2026 is treated as the first decision upon the 
representation dated 13.02.2026, a period of 34 days had 
elapsed before such consideration. A further period of eight 
days elapsed before the rejection was communicated to the 
detenu on 27.03.2026. No separate order deciding the 
representation has been placed before us. Nor has any 
satisfactory or day-to-day explanation been furnished for the 
time taken either to consider the representation or to 
communicate the decision. The general statement that the 
representation was examined together with the opinion of the 
Advisory Board does n ot explain the delay. It instead 
reinforces the conclusion that the representation was not 
treated as an independent constitutional process requiring 
immediate attention. 
 
21) We accordingly hold that the safeguards attaching to the right 
of the detenu to make a representation against his detention 
were not observed. The detenu was not informed of his right 
to represent to the Detaining Authority who had made the 
order. The record does not disclose any independent decision 
upon the representation by the Detaining Authority in 
exercise of his own statutory power. The consideration 
disclosed by the respondents was undertaken only as part of 
the subsequent confirmation exercise, and  even that 
consideration was attended by an unexplained delay. These 
infirmities violate Article 22(5) of the Constitution and are 

--- Page 81 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 13 
 
sufficient to render the continued detention of the detenu 
illegal. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
22) The infirmities noted above are not mere technical or 
procedural irregularities capable of being cured by 
substantial compliance. They concern the enforcement of the 
constitutional right guaranteed by Article 22(5) to a person 
detained without trial. Once a mandatory constitut ional 
safeguard governing preventive detention is found to have 
been violated, the continued detention cannot be sustained . 
The High Court did not examine whether the representation 
submitted by the detenu received the independent and 
expeditious consideration required by Article 22(5) of the 
Constitution. Since that issue bears directly upon the legality 
of the continued deten tion, the judgment of the High Court 
cannot be sustained. 
 
23) Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order 
dated 08.04.2026 passed by the High Court in Writ Petition 
(Criminal) No. 566 of 2026 is set aside. The order of detention 
dated 13.01.2026 passed against the detenu under Section 
3(1) of the PITND PS Act and the order of confirmation dated 
19.03.2026 are quashed. 
 
24) The detenu, Muhammed Rafi, shall be set at liberty forthwith, 
unless his detention or custody is required in connection with 
any other case. 

--- Page 82 ---
CRL.A. NO…./2026@SLP(CRL.) NO.8439 OF 2026 14 
 
 
25) Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. There 
shall be no order as to costs.

interim order was made on 28 th June, 2016 whereby the
following was recorded:
“Heard  learned  Advocate  General  for  the
appellants and Sri K.Raghava Charyulu, learned
counsel for respondent Nos. 3 to 12. 
It is not in dispute that the property in
question is in possession of the State.  Learned
Advocate General makes a statement that the State
shall protect the property till the disposal of
the appeal.
In  the  circumstances,  there  shall  be  ad
interim order as prayed in the WPMP.  It is
needless to mention that the State shall not
create any third party in the property without
permission of the Court.”
8. The said interim order is operating even now.  It
is at this stage, IA No.1 of 2026 came to be filed by the
respondents  herein  before  the  High  Court  which  is
resulted in the impugned order. 
9. The grievance of the petitioner is that they were
not made a party and as such they were also not heard
when the order for survey was made.  
10. Learned  senior  counsel  for  the  contesting
respondents submits that it is the State which is in
appeal and there wa s  no need to hear the petitioner
herein.
11

--- Page 94 ---
11. We are of the considered opinion that interest of
justice will be sub-served, if the following order is
made:
(a) The petitioner will be at liberty to seek
impleadment in the Writ Appeal;
(b) We  record  the  statement  of  Mr.
C.S.Vaidyanathan, learned senior counsel appearing
for the petitioner that along with the application
for impleadment, they will file an application for
modification/clarification/vacation  of  the
impugned order dated 8th July, 2026.  
(c) On such application being filed, the High
Court  shall,  uninfluenced  by  the  observations
made either in the impugned order or in the
present  order,  hear  and  dispose  of  the  said
application;
(d) We further direct that in the event the
Survey has not been held, the status quo will be
maintained and it will await the disposal of the
application  which  the  petitioner  proposes  to
file; and
(e) It  is  made  clear  that  the  protection
available under this order with regard to the
keeping of Survey in abeyance will enure to the
benefit of the petitioner for one week and, in
12

--- Page 95 ---
any event not later than 14 th August, 2026.  If
the petitioner is really serious, by the said
date they will move the necessary application and
bring it up for hearing.
12. Mr.  Shiva  Santosh  Kumar  Yelamanchili,  learned
counsel for the contesting respondents brings to our
notice that the petitioner has already notified auction
of the subject lands.
13. Mr. C.S.Vaidyanathan, learned senior counsel for
the petitioner states that no such proposal to auction
the properties, which are in question in the Writ Appeal,
exists.
14. We record the statement.
15. With  the  above  observations,  the  Special  Leave
Petition is disposed of.
16. Pending application shall stand disposed of.
(ANITA MALHOTRA)                          (MANOJ KUMAR)

O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Respondent Nos.1, 1.1 to 1.3 are served and unrepresented.
Respondent Nos.2 to 8 are proforma respondents who are undisputedly
the plaintiffs before the Court and as such notice stands dispensed
with.
4. By the impugned order, the application filed under Order VII
Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (“CPC”) filed by the
1

--- Page 109 ---
respondents – defendants contending that the appellant – plaintiff
– trust is not registered under the M.P. Public Trust Act, 1951,
therefore, it is not entitled to claim exemption in terms of
notification issued under Section 3(2) of the M.P. Accommodation
Control Act, 1961 and as such suit is not maintainable came to be
accepted and as such the unsuccessful plaintiff – trust is before
this Court.
5. We  have  heard  the  arguments  of  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant.
6. As noticed hereinabove, respondents Nos.1, 1.1 to 1.3 who are
served are unrepresented and as such the matter has been processed
by the Registry for being listed, since this is a direction matter
and the present appeal is of the year 2017 and the original
eviction proceedings relates to year 2010. Hence, we are of the
considered view that keeping this matter further pending would only
add saga to the ordeal already being undergone by the appellant –
trust. Hence, we have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant and we are disposing of this appeal on merits as
it involves a short point, namely, 
“whether  the  plaintiff  was  not  entitled  to  claim
exemption  in  terms  of  Section  3(2)  of  the  M.P.
2

--- Page 110 ---
Accommodation Control Act, 1961?”
7. An Eviction Petition came to be filed by the appellant – trust
against original respondent No.1 (not represented by the legal
representatives;  respondent  Nos.1.1  to  1.3)  for  eviction  and
arrears of rent raising various grounds as more fully stated in the
plaint (Annexure – P-3). On service of suit summons,  defendants
appeared, filed their written statement, denied the averments made
in the plaint and during the course of the pendency of the
proceedings, they filed an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC
for  rejection  of  the  plaint  contending  inter  alia that  the
plaintiff – trust is a public trust declared by notification dated
04.07.1968 issued under sub-section (2) of Section 36 of M.P.
Public Trust Act, 1951 and the property of the plaintiff – trust,
namely, the suit schedule property is situated outside the State
where it is registered, exemption from all such provisions of the
M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961 was given, which was cancelled
by  the  Government  of  Madhya  Pradesh  by  notification  dated
18.09.1971 which has been challenged by the plaintiff – trust
before the High Court in M.P. No.35/1972 and the said notification
came to be maintained by the judgment dated 25.04.1973 and this
3

--- Page 111 ---
order has not been challenged by plaintiff – trust and same has
attained finality. It was contended that Section 3(2) of the M.P.
Accommodation Control Act, 1961 provides for granting exemption
from all Sections or from any sub-section to such educational
institutions, religious or society and in exercise of such power,
the State Government by notification dated 07.09.1989 under the
M.P. Public Trust Act, 1951 have declared educational, religious or
proposed proposal having been registered having all places of
ownership of public trust has declared as exempted from such act.
Hence, contending when plaintiff – trust is not registered under
the M.P. Trust Act, 1951 and as such is not entitled for exemption
under the provisions of M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961 and by
relying upon the notification dated 07.07.1989, the application
came to be filed for rejection of plaint.
8. The  learned  trial  judge  by  the  order  dated  19.03.2012
dismissed the said application. The revision filed assailing the
said order by the defendants resulted in Revision Petition being
allowed by the impugned order dated 06.04.2017, I.A. No.6467/2020
has been filed enclosing therewith notification dated 12.07.2018.
Perusal of the same would indicate that said notification is issued
in exercise of the power conferred under sub-section (2) of Section
4

--- Page 112 ---
3 of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, and it was in
continuation of the notification dated 07.07.1989 which had been
relied  upon  by  the  defendants.  Under  the  notification  dated
12.07.2018, the State Government has exempted any accommodation
situated in the State of Madhya Pradesh owned by the public trust
registered  in  “other  States  of  the  Republic  of  India  for
educational,  religious  or  charitable  purposes  from  all  the
provision of the said Act”. In the light of the subsequent
notification dated 02.07.2018 which was in continuation to the
earlier notification dated 07.07.1989, the finding of the High
Court  under  the  impugned  order  that  the  notification  dated
07.07.1989 would bar the suits being prosecuted by the trust which
are registered outside the State of Madhya Pradesh would not hold
water. On this short ground itself, the impugned order is liable to
be set aside and accordingly, it is set aside and the matter stands
remitted to the jurisdictional Court for being disposed of on
merits and in accordance with the law.
9. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, the
aforestated  order  has  been  passed  keeping  open  all  other
contentions of both parties for being adjudicated. We also make it
clear that the respondents though served and unrepresented, it
5

--- Page 113 ---
would be incumbent upon the trial court to issue notice afresh to
the respondents – defendants before proceeding with the trial and
only after effecting such service of notice or holding service of
notice valid, the suit can be proceeded with and not otherwise.
10. With the aforesaid observations, the appeal is allowed and the
impugned order stands set aside. No order as to costs. All pending
applications stand consigned to records. 
.................J.
  (ARAVIND KUMAR)
.................J.
(PRASANNA B. VARALE)
NEW DELHI;
MARCH 19, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO……………………OF 2026 
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 1494 OF 2025) 
 
MITALI MADHUMITA MALLICK             ...APPELLANT(S) 
VS.  
TAPOMAYA PATTANAYAK                 ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal arises out of the final judgment and 
order dated 8th October,  2024 passed by the High 
Court of Orissa at Cuttack in W.P.(C) No. 22451 of 
2024, whereby the writ petition preferred by the 
appellant-wife seeking pendente lite maintenance from 
the date of filing of the application under Section 24 of 
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 came to be dismissed. 
3. The brief facts necessary for adjudication of the present 
appeal are as follows: 
3.1. The marriage between the petitioner-wife and the 
respondent-husband was solemnised on 4th 
July, 2014 in accordance with Hindu rites and 
customs. The parties have been residing 
separately since 8th September, 2018. 

--- Page 128 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  2 
 
3.2. On 11th February, 2021, an FIR was registered 
at the instance of the petitioner -wife against the 
respondent-husband under Sections 498A, 323, 
506 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and 
Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. 
3.3. The petitioner -wife instituted C.M.C. No. 61 of 
2020 under Section 12 of the Protection of 
Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 before 
the SDJM, Bhubaneswar, and C.P. No. 104 of 
2020 under Sections 12 and 13(1)(ia) of the 
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 before the Family 
Court, Bhubaneswar. She also filed applications 
seeking pendente lite maintenance in both the 
proceedings. 
3.4. In the proceedings arising out of C.M.C. No. 61 of 
2020, by order dated 3rd March, 2023, the JMFC 
(LR), Bhubaneswar  directed the respondent -
husband to pay interim maintenance of 
₹30,000/- per month.  
3.5. By a common order dated 4th October, 2023 
passed in Criminal Appeal Nos. 28 and 37 of 
2023, the Additional Sessions Judge -IV, 
Bhubaneswar enhanced the maintenance to 
₹40,000/- per month with effect from the date of 
filing of the application. 

--- Page 129 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  3 
 
3.6. Aggrieved thereby, the respondent -husband 
preferred Criminal Revision No. 591 of 2023 
before the High Court. By judgment dated 5th 
December, 2023, the High Court set aside the 
appellate order, restored the order dated 3rd 
March, 2023 passed by the JMFC (LR), 
Bhubaneswar, and held that the petitioner -wife 
would be entitled to interim maintenance from 
7th June, 2022, being the date of filing of the 
application under Section 23 of the Protection of 
Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. 
3.7. In the matrimonial proceedings, namely C.P. No. 
104 of 2020 instituted under Sections 12 and 
13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the 
Family Court, Bhubaneswar, by order dated 30th 
March, 2024, rejected I.A. No. 24 of 2021 filed by 
the petitioner -wife under Section 24 of the Act 
seeking pendente lite maintenance. Aggrieved 
thereby, the petitioner-wife preferred W.P.(C) No. 
22451 of 2024 before the High Court. 
4. The High Court, vide the impugned judgment and 
order, dismissed the writ petition holding that the 
petitioner-wife had instituted C.M.C. No. 61 of 2020 
under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence 

--- Page 130 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  4 
 
Act, 2005 prior to filing I.A. No. 24 of 2021 under 
Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The High 
Court further noted that the order dated 3rd March,  
2023 passed by the JMFC (LR), Bhubaneswar granting 
interim maintenance had already been restored by the 
High Court in Criminal Revision No. 591 of 2023 by 
judgment dated 5th December, 2023. In view thereof, it 
held that the petitioner's claim for grant of maintenance 
under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 from 
an earlier date could not be entertained and, 
accordingly, dismissed the writ petition. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and 
perused the material available on record. 
6. During the pendency of the present appeal, by order 
dated 3rd November, 2025, this Court referred the 
parties to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre for 
exploring the possibility of an amicable settlement. 
Pursuant thereto, the parties participated in the 
mediation proceedings and entered into a Settlement 
Agreement dated 10th January, 2026. 
7. A joint application, being I.A. No. 150975 of 2026, has 
been filed under Article 142 of the Constitution placing 
the Settlement Agreement on record and praying for 

--- Page 131 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  5 
 
dissolution of the marriage by mutual consent and for 
quashing of all pending proceedings between the 
parties. 
8. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and 
interacted with the parties, who are present before the 
Court. They affirm that the settlement has been arrived 
at voluntarily, of their own free will, and without any 
coercion, undue influence or fraud. The parties have 
unequivocally stated that there is no possibility of 
reconciliation and have mutually agreed to dissolve 
their marriage. 
9. The salient terms of the Settlement Agreement are as 
follows: 
i) The parties have agreed to dissolve their marriage by 
mutual consent by invoking the jurisdiction of this 
Court under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, 
there being no possibility of reconciliation. 
ii) The respondent-husband has agreed to pay a sum 
of ₹38,50,000/- (Rupees Thirty -Eight Lakhs and 
Fifty Thousand only), excluding the maintenance 
already paid pursuant to the orders passed in the 
proceedings between the parties, towards full and 
final settlement of all claims of the appellant -wife, 
including p ermanent alimony, maintenance, 

--- Page 132 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  6 
 
stridhan and all other claims arising out of the 
matrimonial dispute. 
iii) The settlement amount was payable in two 
installments, namely ₹13,00,000/- and 
₹25,50,000/-. Both instalments have been duly paid 
by the respondent -husband and acknowledged by 
the appellant-wife. 
iv) The parties have exchanged and returned all 
ornaments and jewellery in accordance with the 
terms of the Settlement Agreement. 
v) The parties have agreed for quashing of all pending 
civil and criminal proceedings arising out of their 
matrimonial relationship. 
vi) The parties have agreed that neither of them shall 
initiate any further civil or criminal proceedings 
against the other or against the members of their 
respective families in relation to the matrimonial 
dispute. 
vii) The parties have agreed that they have no further 
claim or demand against each other, including in 
respect of maintenance, permanent alimony, 
stridhan, movable or immovable property, or any 
other claim arising out of their matrimonial 
relationship. 

--- Page 133 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  7 
 
10. We are satisfied that the Settlement Agreement has 
been voluntarily executed and that its terms are lawful. 
Having regard to the fact that the parties have been 
residing separately since 8th September, 2018, that all 
their disputes have been amicably resol ved through 
mediation before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre, 
and that they have unequivocally expressed their desire 
to bring their matrimonial relationship to an end, we 
are of the considered view that this is a fit case for 
exercise of our plenary powers under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India to do complete justice between the 
parties and bring a quietus to all disputes and litigation 
arising out of their matrimonial relationship. 
11. Accordingly, I.A. No. 150975 of 2026 is allowed. In view 
of the Settlement Agreement and in exercise of our 
powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, 
we pass the following directions: 
(i) The marriage solemnised between the petitioner-wife 
Mithali Madhumita Mallick and the respondent -
husband Tapomaya Pattanayak on 4th July, 2014 
stands dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual 
consent. 
(ii) All pending civil and criminal proceedings instituted 
by either party against the other, or against the 

--- Page 134 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  8 
 
members of their respective families, arising out of 
the matrimonial dispute, shall stand quashed and 
shall be deemed to have been finally disposed of. 
These include, inter alia: 
(a) C.P. No. 104 of 2020 pending before the Family 
Court-I, Bhubaneswar; 
(b) C.M.C. No. 61 of 2020 pending before the JMFC 
(LR), Bhubaneswar; 
(c) C.T. Case No. 923 of 2021 arising out of P.S. Case 
No. 17 of 2021 pending before the SDJM, 
Bhubaneswar; 
(d) W.P. No. 12391 of 2025 pending before the High 
Court of Orissa; and 
(e) W.P. No. 16320 of 2025 pending before the High 
Court of Orissa. 
12. Both parties, who are present before this Court, have 
affirmed that they shall abide by the terms and 
conditions of the Settlement Agreement and shall not 
raise any further claims or initiate any civil or criminal 
proceedings against each other or against the members 
of their respective families in relation to the 
matrimonial dispute. 

--- Page 135 ---
C.A. …../2026@ SLP (C) NO. 1494/2025  9 
 
13. The present appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid 
terms. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand 
disposed of. Registry shall communicate this order to 
all the concerned Court s where the matters were 
pending and have been quashed by this order. Formal 
orders may be passed by the respective Courts closing 
the proceedings . Registry shall also d raw the decree 
accordingly.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 34219 of 2025)
RAMA & ORS.                                    APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
KEDAR & ANR.                                  RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The deceased Kailash, an electrician and
electric motor repair mechanic (motor rewinding
mechanic), died in a road accident on 06.01.2022.
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal allowed a
compensation  of  Rs.17,84,215/-  taking  his
notional income at Rs.8,435/- per month.
3. On  appeal  before  the  High  Court,  the
notional income has been enhanced to Rs.11,035/-
per  month.  Both  the  Courts  have  allowed
compensation on other heads, however, in this
appeal, we are not concerned with the amount of
compensation awarded to the appellant(s) on other
heads, as the arguments before us remain confined
to the determination of the notional income of
1

--- Page 161 ---
the deceased.
4. Ms. Ishita M. Puranik, learned counsel for the
appellant(s)  would  submit  that  the  notional
income of the deceased ought to be taken at
Rs.20,000/- per month, keeping in view the fact
that the deceased was a qualified motor rewinding
mechanic.
5. Per  contra,  Mr.  Vishal  Meghwal,  learned
counsel  appearing  for  respondent  No.2  would
submit that there is no material on record to
substantiate  that  the  deceased  was  earning
Rs.20,000/- per month. It is further submitted
that the High Court has adequately enhanced the
compensation by taking the deceased's notional
income at Rs.11,035/- per month and there is no
scope for further enhancement.
6. The appeal papers would include a vocational
training certificate issued by the Industrial
Training  Institute  (ITI),  Sendhwa,  District
Barwani (M.P.) in the year 2005–2006, certifying
that the deceased had received theoretical and
practical training as an electrician and electric
motor repair professional as a regular trainee
for one year from 01.07.2005 to 30.06.2006.
7. The appellant(s) also relied on a circular
dated  05.10.2021  issued  by  the  Labour
Commissioner,  Barwani  (M.P.),  notifying  the
2

--- Page 162 ---
monthly wages of a highly skilled workman at
Rs.12,335/- per month. Thus, it appears that the
minimum  wage  admissible  to  a  highly  skilled
individual  was  fixed  by  the  Government  at
Rs.12,335/- per month.
8. The issue now remains to be considered is
whether the deceased should be treated as a
skilled person or a highly skilled person. As per
the Notification dated 30.12.2025 issued by the
Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of
India, a highly skilled occupation has been duly
defined in the following manner:
...”(i)  highly  skilled
occupation” means an occupation
which calls in its performance a
specific level of perfection and
required  competence  acquired
through  intensive  technical  or
professional  training  or
practical occupational experience
for  a  considerable  period  and
also requires of an employee to
assume  full  responsibility  for
his judgment or decision involved
in  the  execution  of  such
occupation;”
9. The job profile of the deceased, a motor
rewinding mechanic, who holds a qualification
certificate  issued  by  an  Industrial  Training
Center (ITI) of the State Government, shows that
3

--- Page 163 ---
he has definitely achieved a specific level of
perfection in conducting the specialized work of
a motor rewinding mechanic. There is a distinct
difference between a skilled person (such as a
carpenter, etc.) and another skilled person who
possesses formal technical qualifications and has
experience of more than 15 years of performing
the work of a motor rewinding mechanic.
10. In our considered view, the deceased can be
treated  as  belonging  to  a  highly  skilled
occupation, for which the notional income of
Rs.12,335/-  per  month  can  indeed  be  made
applicable.
11. Thus, we hold that the notional income of
the  deceased  taken  by  the  High  Court  at
Rs.11,035/-  per  month  should  be  enhanced  to
Rs.12,335/-  per  month,  and  the  amount  of
compensation on this particular head deserves to
be recalculated.
12. Learned  counsel  for  the  parties  would
jointly  submit  that  upon  recalculating  the
enhanced  notional  income,  the  enhanced
compensation liability comes to Rs. 2,60,442/-.
At  this  stage,  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant(s)  further  submits  that  the
appellant(s) deserves 10 per cent increase on
conventional  heads  and  the  appellant(s)  are
4

--- Page 164 ---
entitled to an additional sum of Rs.27,000/-.
13. Considering the above factors, including the
increase in notional income and 10 per cent
increase  in  conventional  heads  as  per  the
principles laid down in “ National Insurance Co.
Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.”1, we direct that the
appellant(s) would be entitled to a lump-sum
additional compensation of Rs.2,75,000/- (Rupees
Two Lakh Seventy-Five Thousand Only) along with
interest from the date of application before the
Claims Tribunal. Let this enhanced amount be
deposited  by  the  respondent-Insurance  Company
before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal within
three months. 
14. Accordingly, the Appeal is allowed in part in
the above terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 1 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS……………………..OF 2026 
(@SLP(CRIMINAL) NOS. 10423-10424 OF 2026) 
 
SIDDALINGAPPAGOUDA BIRADAR  ...APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
SHANTAPPA & ORS.               ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Leave granted.  
 
2. The present appeals arise out of the common judgment and 
order dated 09.04.2026 passed by the High Court  of 
Karnataka at Kalaburgi in Criminal Petition Nos. 200495 of 
2026 and 200500 of 2026, whereby the High Court granted 
regular bail to Accused Nos. 3 to 5 and anticipatory bail to 
Accused Nos. 1, 2 and 6 to 9 in connection with Crime No. 
87 of 2026. For convenience, the respondents shall 
hereinafter be referred to by their respective positions as 
accused in Crime No. 87 of 2026. 
 
3. The brief facts giving rise to the appeals are as follows:  
3.1. FIR No. 87/2026 came to be registered on 10.03.2026 
at the instance of the appellant at Police Station 

--- Page 168 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 2 
 
Muddebihal, Vijayapura District, for offences 
punishable under Sections 189(2), 191(2), 191(3), 
115(2), 118(1), 118(2), 331(1), 352 and 351(2) read with 
Section 190 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 1. 
During the course of investigation, Section 109 of the 
BNS also came to be added. 
3.2. The FIR reveals that on 10.03.2026 at about 10:30 a.m., 
the accused persons  entered the residence of the 
appellant armed with iron rods  and wooden logs,  and 
assaulted the appellant's father, Sh. Shantagouda 
Biradar. The FIR further alleges that the assault was the 
culmination of an existing dispute arising from his 
father's intervention as a mediator in a land dispute 
between the respondents and their own brothers about 
six months ago.  
3.3. The record reflects that the appellant’s father sustained 
multiple fractures, including fractures of the right 
fibula, proximal tibia, right patella, right hip and ribs. 
He underwent multiple surgeries. The appellant's aunt 
and differently abled  sister, who allegedly intervened 
during the assault, also sustained injuries. 
 
1 In short, BNS.  

--- Page 169 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 3 
 
3.4. Accused Nos. 1, 2 and 6 to 9 preferred Criminal Misc. 
No. 5021 of 2026 seeking anticipatory bail, whereas 
Accused Nos. 3 to 5 preferred Criminal Misc. No. 5022 
of 2026 seeking regular bail before the Court of the V 
Additional District and Sessions Judge, Vijayapura.  By 
separate orders dated 04.04.2026, the Sessions Court 
rejected the applications, taking note of the nature of 
the allegations, the injuries sustained by the appellant's 
father and the fact that he continued to remain 
hospitalised. Even at the time the bail applications were 
considered by the Trial Court and the High Court, he 
was hospitalised.  
3.5. Aggrieved, the accused persons  preferred Criminal 
Petition Nos. 200500 of 2026 and 200495 of 2026 before 
the High Court. By a common judgment and order dated 
09.04.2026, the High Court allowed both petitions, 
granting anticipatory bail to Accused Nos. 1, 2 and 6 to 
9 and regular bail to Accused Nos. 3 to 5. 
3.6. Aggrieved thereby, the appellant is before this Court. 
 
4. We have heard the parties and examined the material placed 
on record.  
 

--- Page 170 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 4 
 
5. It is a well settled proposition that an order granting bail 
undoubtedly need not contain elaborate reasons. Equally, 
where a reasoned order refusing bail is sought to be 
reversed, the appellate court is expected to indicate, at least 
briefly, the circumstan ces which persuaded it to take a 
different view. The impugned order, in our considered 
opinion, does not satisfy this requirement. 
 
6. The Sessions Court denied anticipatory bail and regular bail 
to the accused persons  after clearly noting the serious 
nature of allegations and the kind of injuries sustained by 
appellant’s father, which were caused by iron rods. It further 
noted that he sustained five fractures of different bones and 
is still undergoing treatment. It also noted that the accused 
persons would be needed for investigation, as the weapons 
have to be recovered.   
 
7. The High Court, while reversing the orders, has assigned no 
reason other than observing the following:  
“considering the nature and gravity of the 
offences and previous antecedents of the 
petitioners, it is just and proper to allow these 
petitions with conditions.” 
 
This, in our opinion, can hardly be regarded as adequate 
reasoning for grant of bail, that too in a case as grave as this. 

--- Page 171 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 5 
 
The impugned order does not indicate what weighed with the 
High Court in taking a view contrary to that taken by the 
Sessions Court. Reference is not made either to the nature 
of the allegations,  or the role attributed to the individual 
accused persons, or the medical condition of the injured. 
 
8. The material placed on record clearly suggests that the 
appellant’s father had to undergo multiple surgeries and 
treatments. The Sessions Court recorded that he continued 
to remain under treatment while considering the bail 
applications. We also find that the High Court appears to 
have proceeded on the submission that the injured was in a 
stable condition and out of danger. The medical certificate 
dated 03.04.2026, however, records that he had sustained 
multiple fractures, had undergone multiple surgeries and 
continued to remain admitted in the hospital. The appellant 
has further placed material before this Court alleging that, 
subsequent to their release, the respondents threatened the 
appellant and his father, leading to registration of NCR No. 
54 of 2026. 
 
9. We cannot overlook the manner in which the bail 
applications dated 07.04.2026 came to be decided. The Trial 
Court rejected the bail applications on 04.04.2026. Within 
five days thereafter, the High Court reversed the order on 

--- Page 172 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 6 
 
09.04.2026. On that day , the Court directed the learned 
Government Pleader to accept notice for the State and 
proceeded to allow both the application s on the same day . 
The prosecution was thus afforded no effective opportunity 
to place the relevant material before the Court. This becomes 
significant particularly in view of what we have noticed 
above regarding the medical condition of the injured.  
 
10. At this stage, we refrain from expressing any final opinion 
on these rival assertions. Nevertheless, these were material 
circumstances which required due consideration while 
deciding the bail applications. 
 
11. In view of the foregoing, we are satisfied that the impugned 
order granting bail suffers from non-application of mind and 
cannot be sustained. The impugned common judgment and 
order dated 09.04.2026 is accordingly set aside. 
 
12. All the applications for anticipatory bail and regular bail are 
restored to their original numbers before the High Court, to 
be heard and decided on merits after affording due 
opportunities to the parties. 
  
13. The accused persons who have been granted bail by the 
impugned order shall surrender within four weeks from 

--- Page 173 ---
CRL. A. …./2026@SLP(CRL.) NOS.10423-10424/2026 7 
 
today and their bail applications be considered afresh by the 
High Court only after they surrender and file its proof.  
 
14. Accordingly, the appeals are allowed.  
 
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Delay condoned.
2. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits that he would not
press the appeal against Respondent No.5 herein. Submission is placed
on  record.  Accordingly,  the  appeal  against  Respondent  No.5  stands
dismissed as not pressed. He further submits that Respondent No. 7 is
said to have expired and seeks leave of the court to amend the cause
title by incorporating name of the legal representatives of the deceased
Respondent No.7 on record.

  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY JURISDICTION
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (C) NO.   24580    OF 2026  
AMIT KUMAR SINGH                                 PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND & ANR.                   RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
We have heard learned senior counsel for the petitioner. 
The advertisement for the recruitment to the post of  
Grade-IV in the Court of Principal District and Sessions  
Judge,  Dhanbad  was  issued  in  the  year  2023  and  the  
recruitment was concluded and the select list and waiting 
list  of successful candidates were issued vide Office Order 
No.346/2023  dated 22.11.2023.
Learned senior counsel Dr. Shashi Kiran appearing for the
petitioner  submitted  that  in  the  advertisement  in  the  
reservation  matrix,  there  was  no  provision  made  for  
horizontal reservation for the disabled persons as mandated
under Section 34 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities  
Act, 2016 (For short, `the 2016 Act’).  She  therefore,  
submitted that the petitioner herein has been deprived of 
being selected in the recruitment in that category. 
In this regard, learned senior counsel pointed out that 
under Section 34 of the 2016 Act, not less than four per cent
1

--- Page 205 ---
of the total number of vacancies in the cadre strength in 
each group of posts are meant to be filled with persons with 
benchmark disabilities.
For immediate reference, Section 34 of the  2016 Act is 
extracted as under -
“34.  Reservation.—(1)  Every  appropriate  Government
shall appoint in every Government establishment, not
less than four per cent. of the total number of
vacancies in the cadre strength in each group of posts
meant  to  be  filled  with  persons  with  benchmark
disabilities of which, one per cent. each shall be
reserved for persons with benchmark disabilities under
clauses (a), (b) and (c) and one per cent. for persons
with benchmark disabilities under clauses (d) and (e),
namely:—
(a) blindness and low vision; 
(b) deaf and hard of hearing; 
 (c) locomotor disability including cerebral palsy, 
leprosy cured, dwarfism, acid attack victims and
muscular dystrophy;
(d)  autism,  intellectual  disability,  specific
learning disability and mental illness;
(e) multiple disabilities from amongst persons under
clauses (a) to (d) including deaf-blindness in the
posts identified for each disabilities: 
Provided that the reservation in promotion shall be in
accordance with such instructions as are issued by the
appropriate Government from time to time: 
Provided further that the appropriate Government, in
consultation with the Chief Commissioner or the State
Commissioner, as the case may be, may, having regard to
the  type  of  work  carried  out  in  any  Government
establishment, by notification and subject to such
conditions,  if  any,  as  may  be  specified  in  such
notifications exempt any Government establishment from
the provisions of this section. 
(2) Where in any recruitment year any vacancy cannot be
filled up due to non-availability of a suitable person
with benchmark disability or for any other sufficient
reasons, such vacancy shall be carried forward in the
succeeding recruitment year and if in the succeeding
recruitment year also suitable person with benchmark
disability is not available, it may first be filled by
interchange among the five categories and only when
there is no person with disability available for the
2

--- Page 206 ---
post in that year, the employer shall fill up the
vacancy by appointment of a person, other than a person
with  disability:  Provided  that  if  the  nature  of
vacancies in an establishment is such that a given
category of person cannot be employed, the vacancies
may be interchanged among the five categories with the
prior approval of the appropriate Government. 
(3) The appropriate Government may, by notification,
provide for such relaxation of upper age limit for
employment of persons with benchmark disability, as it
thinks fit.”
Alternatively, learned senior counsel appearing for
the petitioner submitted that in case this Court is not
inclined to interfere with the impugned recruitment, the
Jharkhand High Court as well as State of Jharkhand may be
directed to make provision for horizontal reservation as per
Section 34 of the 2016 Act.
Learned senior counsel also drew our attention to
paragraph 50 of the judgment passed in Union of India and
Anr. vs. National Federation of the Blind and Ors. (2013) 10
SCC 772, which reads as under -
“50. Employment is a key factor in the empowerment
and inclusion of people with disabilities. It is an
alarming reality that the disabled people are out
of job not because their disability comes in the
way of their functioning rather it is social and
practical barriers that prevent them from joining
the workforce. As a result, many disabled people
live in poverty and in deplorable conditions. They
are denied the right to make a useful contribution
to their own lives and to the lives of their
families and community.”
The said paragraph emphasises the fact that one of
the ways of empowerment of persons with disabilities is
providing employment. 
3

--- Page 207 ---
Taking note of the above provision as well as what
has been stated by this Court in the aforesaid judgment, we
direct that the State of Jharkhand as well as the Jharkhand
High Court shall take steps to provide for horizontal
reservation in terms of Section 34 of the 2016 Act in all
recruitments in future, if not already provided.
The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
aforesaid terms. 
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.
A copy of this order may be sent to the Chief
Secretary, State of Jharkhand by the Registry of this
Court. 
     ……………………………………………J.
[B.V. NAGARATHNA]
……………………………………………J.
        [R. MAHADEVAN]
 NEW DELHI
 JULY 31, 2026
4

AMAN KUMAR @ AMAN YADAV      APPELLANT(S)

STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant;
learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Haryana;
and learned counsel for Respondent No.2-informant.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
06.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana  at  Chandigarh  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’
hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail application of
the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  FIR  No.149/2024
registered at Police Station- Khedki Daula, District-
Gurugram, Haryana under Sections 406, 420 and 180 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
5. Core accusation against the appellant is that he
1

--- Page 223 ---
and the informant were in a business relationship in
terms of which a joint account was opened in the
concerned Bank. According to the informant, one day in
the month of the February, 2018, when he visited the
Bank, i.e. the ICICI Bank, to ascertain the details of
the joint account, he found that the appellant did not
deposit any amount but the entire deposits made by the
informant into the joint account have been transferred
by the appellant to his personal account and those of
his relatives.
6. This Court vide order dated 23.06.2026 had issued
notice  pursuant  to  which  Respondent  No.1-State  of
Haryana has filed counter affidavit. On being added as
Respondent  No.2,  informant  has  also  filed  counter
affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
there is inordinate delay of more than 04 years in
lodging of the First Information Report. The police had
thoroughly investigated the matter and had come to a
conclusion that it was a civil dispute and had filed
closure report. During the entire period, appellant had
co-operated with the investigation. It was only after
the Magistrate had directed re-investigation that the
appellant came to be arrested on 09.12.2025 and since
then, he has been in custody. Learned counsel has also
2

--- Page 224 ---
made submissions on merit.
8. Learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.1-State  of
Haryana has referred to the counter affidavit filed by
the State of Haryana and submits that the trial has
commenced,  whereafter  11  out  of  19  prosecution
witnesses have been examined. The trial is proceeding
satisfactorily. Therefore, at this stage, appellant may
not be enlarged on bail.
9. Learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.2-informant
submits that it is a clear case of cheating by the
appellant. That apart, he has also tried to influence a
prosecution witness. If the appellant is enlarged on
bail, there is a possibility that he will try to
influence the witnesses. Therefore, appellant may not
be enlarged on bail, at this stage.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, we find that appellant is in
custody  for  more  than  06  months  now.  The  charges
against the appellant are magistrate triable. During
the course of initial investigation by the police,
there is no allegation that appellant did not join the
investigation.  He  came  to  be  arrested  only  after
the  Magistrate  directed  re-investigation.  In  the
circumstances, we are of the view that a case for bail
is made out.
3

--- Page 225 ---
11. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 06.05.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced  before  the  concerned  Magistrate  within  a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate. We also make it clear
that  if  the  appellant  tries  to  influence  the
prosecution witnesses who are yet to depose, the State
of Haryana would be at liberty to seek cancellation of
bail. Further, we direct that the appellant shall not
seek unnecessary adjournment in the ongoing trial.
12. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.
13. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
